    AI Overview
    The Artemis II mission is scheduled to splash down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, California, on Friday, April 10, 2026, at approximately 8:07 p.m. EDT (5:07 p.m. PDT). The crew, returning from a 10-day lunar flyby, will be recovered by the USS John P. Murtha. 
    Key Details for Splashdown: 
    • Date: Friday, April 10, 2026
    • Time: 8:07 p.m. EDT / 5:07 p.m. PDT
    • Location: Pacific Ocean, off the coast of San Diego, CA
    • Coverage: Live on NASA's YouTube channel, Netflix, and NASA+ beginning around 6:30 p.m. EDT 
    Return Sequence (April 10): 
    • 4:33 p.m. PDT (7:33 p.m. EDT): Service module separation
    • 4:53 p.m. PDT (7:53 p.m. EDT): Entry interface (beginning of re-entry)
    • ~5:07 p.m. PDT (8:07 p.m. EDT): Parachute deployment and splashdown

    Astrophysicist & science communicator
    Artemis II is scheduled to reenter Earth’s atmosphere on April 10, 2026, with splashdown planned in the Pacific Ocean later that day local time, or April 11 in UTC. The Orion spacecraft approaches from the west on a free-return trajectory, keeping the entire reentry corridor over open ocean. This reduces risk and allows recovery forces to be pre-positioned along the flight path. Lunar return reentry occurs at roughly 11 km/s, far faster than low Earth orbit missions. For Artemis II, NASA plans a direct reentry profile rather than a skip, prioritising predictable heating and flight dynamics following analysis of Artemis I. The timings shown here track the final phase from atmospheric interface to splashdown. This ground track was generated by Heavens-Above using published mission parameters, so it represents a modeled trajectory rather than a confirmed final path.

    San Diego is about to be the center of the space world. This Friday, April 10, around 5pm, NASA’s Artemis II astronauts are scheduled to splash down in the Pacific just off our coastline. It marks the first time in more than 50 years that humans return from deep space near San Diego. The crew launched April 1 from Florida, traveling farther from Earth than any humans since Apollo before looping around the Moon and heading home. Their recovery will be handled by the USS John P. Murtha, a San Diego-based Navy vessel many locals have already spotted offshore over the past couple weeks as it trained for this exact moment. After splashdown around 5:08pm, Navy divers and helicopters will secure the Orion capsule and transport the astronauts onto the ship, all happening just beyond the horizon.     They’re coming home. The Artemis II crew returns to Earth tomorrow — here’s everything you need to know. When is splashdown? 🌊 Expected: Friday, April 10 at 5:07 pm PDT 🇦🇺 That’s 10:07 am AEST on Saturday for Australia’s east coast. (Quick tip: Google “5:07 pm PDT to your timezone” for your local time.) Where can you watch it? Live coverage will be available on NASA platforms like NASA+, plus services like Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV, Netflix, HBO Max, and NASA’s YouTube channel. What happens before splashdown? 🚀 ~24 hours before: Final correction burn adjusts their path home. 🛰 42 minutes before: Crew module separates from the service module. 🔥 13 minutes before: They hit Earth’s atmosphere — expect up to 6 minutes of radio silence as plasma forms around the capsule. 🪂 ~3 minutes before: Parachutes deploy. 🌊 Splashdown: After 10 days in space, they return home.
